newsitem.title: UK: Sterling pounded as rate rise expectations fade.
newsitem.headline: Sterling pounded as rate rise expectations fade.

text.p: Sterling took a hammering on Tuesday as expectations of a near-term rise in British interest rates faded in the wake of an apparent softening of the Bank of England's hawkish stance on inflation.

"People are reassessing the interest rate outlook and deciding that rates are almost certainly not going to rise ahead of the general election, and perhaps not even going up this year as far as people have expected," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
On Monday Bank of England governor Eddie George said a spate of economic data alongside sterling's strength had made the need for an interest rate rise less urgent than was thought in December.
The comment made the move in sterling one-way traffic all through the day, making it nose-dive four pfennigs against the mark and two cents against the dollar.
The pound was at 2.7110 marks, down from its day's high of 2.7535 and its late Monday European level of 2.7451. It was at $1.5995 against a high of $1.6175 and Monday's level of $1.6171.

George denied his comment was a softening of the central bank's line but said it was possible that strong sterling could push underlying inflation down to the government's 2.5 percent target in the months ahead. The underlying rate stood at 3.1 percent on a year-on-year basis in January.

But the market did see George's comment as a softening of his previously hard line on rates, which since the last base rate rise -- 0.25 percent to 6.00 last October -- have been strongly resisted by Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke.
Political considerations have stayed Clarke's hand on a politically unpopular monetary tightening ahead of the forthcoming election, which is widely expected to be held on May 1, analysts said.
With sterling having crashed through some strong support levels on its way on Tuesday, traders saw it slipping further, or at least having a struggle to rise back up again.

"It looked like 2.7400 marks would provide some support but it didn't hold. So that may prove to be a bit of an obstacle coming back up, and there may be some selling on rallies," said one trader at a British bank.
Some analysts said data showing the British public sector's borrowing situation was better than expected also added to sterling's weakness.

January public sector debt repayment was 5.818 billion sterling, higher than forecasts of 3.5 billion. January cumulative public sector borrowing requirements were 10.342 billion sterling against 19.336 billion a year ago.

UK Chancellor Kenneth Clarke, lauding the data as "excellent", said Britain was comfortably on the track to achieving its budget forecast for public finances, adding that it may do even better than forecast.

"Sterling's weakness today in part reflects the spectacularly good PSBR data and the perception that fiscal policy was a bit tighter than people had thought, as that releases some of the pressure for higher interest rates," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel.
Meanwhile, the market had discounted the victory by Britain's ruling Conservative Party late on Monday on a censure motion over the government's management of the mad cow disease crisis.
